title: Are "book looks" a waste of time? 2026
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer argues that "book looks" -- the practice of school leaders scrutinizing student exercise books during learning walks -- have become a blunt accountability tool that rewards superficial presentation over evidence of real learning. He opens with an anecdote about a school where leaders equated messy, ink-stained work with poor teaching and neat, copied notes with good teaching, when in fact the "messy" book showed a student actually thinking through independent practice while the "neat" book was just copied notes. Boxer traces the fixation on marking and book presentation to a Department for Education and EEF-driven reduction in excessive marking demands, but argues schools have simply replaced one superficial proxy with another. He rejects the common defense that books need to be tidy because students will use them as revision guides, pointing out that students rarely revisit their books, that reviewing notes is a weak revision strategy compared to retrieval practice, and that printed notes plus practice would be more efficient anyway. Instead, he proposes using books as one data point triangulated against lesson observations, curriculum plans, and conversations with teachers, focusing on what the work reveals about thinking rather than how neat it looks. Used this way, book looks can be genuinely useful; used as a top-down accountability checklist for tidiness, they are close to worthless.
points: Book scrutinies should judge evidence of independent practice and thinking, not surface neatness -- a messy book showing real work beats a tidy book of copied notes.
The DfE and EEF's push to reduce excessive marking removed one superficial teacher-accountability proxy, but many schools simply substituted book presentation as the new one.
Students rarely reuse exercise books as revision guides, and rereading notes is a weak strategy anyway, undercutting the "books are mini revision guides" justification for tidiness.
Book looks are most useful as one data point triangulated with lesson observations, curriculum plans, and conversations with teachers and leaders -- not as a stand-alone verdict.
Departmental autonomy matters: what a "good" book looks like should be negotiated with subject specialists rather than imposed as one uniform standard.
quotes: The first book, on the other hand, is a total mess. The underlining is wobbly, there are spelling mistakes, the handwriting is dreadful and the student has scribbled on the book to get the ink in their pen flowing. But, and this is the crucial point, the first student has actually done some work.

The problem is that we aren't very good at moving on from bad ideas. Marking in exercise books became popular as a proxy for teacher quality because it was obviously visible, easily enforced, and straightforwardly turned into a policy.
Students rarely use their exercise books again. Most never go back to them. Ordinarily, students throw them away or bury them in a cupboard somewhere.

To me, books are used for students as a thinking tool. A way of concretising nascent thoughts through independent practice, and doing spaced retrieval over time. They aren't revision guides and they aren't textbooks.
I do look in exercise books when I'm observing or doing a learning walk. But I try to think about the actual learning, rather than the surface details.
Exercise books are a useful source of data. But they need to be triangulated with other sources, and we need to have questions about learning, rather than presentation, at the forefront of our minds.

When executed with these variables in mind, book looks can be an extremely useful tool. When they are used as a blunt instrument for top-down accountability, they are, at best, a complete waste of time.
